Unde etiam à Pontificiis Articulus hic, dictis verbis constans, simpliciter admissus fertur ab Historiographis Augustanae Confessionis omnibus. Quod ad posteriorem verò mutationem attinet, ignotum esse haud potest, & similem, imò prolixiorem multò improbationem omissam deprehendi in Augustanae Confessionis invariatae Exemplaribus Chytraei & Caelestini, inter se collatis, quoad Articulum XIII. & XVIII. (Quae tamen Omissio nihil prohibuit, quò minus ab Invariatae Confessionis Theologis utrumque Exemplar pro genuino habitum semper sit, hodièque habeatur.) & in plurimis Articulis e.g. in 3. 4. 6. 7. 11. 14. 18. 19. 20. 21. ne a prima quidem Aug. Confessionis adornatione improbationem contrariorum adjectam, nihilominus subaudiendam fuisse.
english: As for the other change — or rather the omission in the Variata of And they reject those who teach otherwise — we admit those exact words are not read there.
Yet in every article of any confession the same sense, or something like it, must be understood: whoever positively confesses a point always denies and rejects what stands against it.
So the omission is only an avoidance of tautology; it can introduce no substantial mutation.

I pass over this further note on the prior change: in the prototype exemplar of the Invariata as the German plainly shows, and Dorsche does not deny it page 183, the article was expressed thus — Concerning the Lord's Supper they confess that the body and blood of Christ are truly present under the species of bread and wine — which at that time could easily smell of pontifical transubstantiation by itself.
Hence the historiographers of the Augsburg Confession report that the pontificals simply admitted this article in those words.

And as for the later omission, it is no secret that a similar — indeed much longer — rejection is missing in the Invariata exemplars of Chytraeus and Caelestinus when Article XIII and XVIII are compared; yet that omission never kept Invariata theologians from treating either exemplar as genuine then or now.
In many articles besides — 3, 4, 6, 7, 11, 14, 18, 19, 20, 21 — no rejection of contrary teaching was added even at the Confession's first framing, and yet it was still to be heard as implied.

source_text: POSTERIUS verò à nobis probandum, scil. mutationem praesertim priorem, Calvinianae Sententiae nullâ ex parte magis favere, quam ipse Articulus invariatus ei favet, sic illucescit: Quia cumprimis Calvinus, Reformatorum Doctoribus annumeratus, & cum Calvino Reformatae Ecclesiae omnes, & veram praesentiam, & veram distributionem Corporis & Sanguinis Christi, in S. Coena admittunt, non minùs quam veram exhibitionem, istasque propter hanc, quam nusquam non inculcant seriò, Signa Sacramentalia, non nude Significantia, sed & Exhibentia, confessi. Justas: At, sub Variatae Confessionis verbis, quibus Corpus & Sanguis Christi, nudè exhiberi, non autem adesse & distribui dicuntur, occultare facilius Calvinianos sententiam suam de Spirituali Corporis & Sanguinis Christi exhibitione posse, ut dum exhiberi ista dicunt verè, Spiritualiter duntaxat exhiberi doceant?
english: The second point we must prove — that the change, especially the prior one, favors the Calvinian sense no more than the unvaried article itself does — comes clear this way.

Calvin, counted among the Reformed doctors, and with him all the Reformed churches, admit a true presence and a true distribution of Christ's body and blood in the holy Supper, no less than a true exhibition.
And because of that exhibition, which they never fail to press, they confess the sacramental signs to be not bare signs only, but also exhibiting signs.

Fair enough. But the charge runs: under the Variata's words, where body and blood are said only to be exhibited, not to be present and distributed, Calvinists can more easily hide a merely spiritual exhibition — saying truly exhibited while teaching exhibited only spiritually.

source_text: Resp. (1.) Idem facere posse Calvinianos in verbis Invariatae Confessionis, ut dum dicunt: Corpus & Sanguinem Christi verè adesse & distribui, illa spiritualiter tantum adesse & distribui intelligant. (2.) Etiam invariatae solius Confessores, Spiritualem praesentiam pariter atque distributionem, haud magis quàm Exhibitionem ac Manducationem Spiritualem, inficiari, praesertim cum & suam Corporalem praesentiam, Distributionem, Manducationem & Exhibitionem, hyperphysicas nihilominus & Supernaturales inculcent esse. (3.) Non nudam Spiritualem praesentiam, Distributionem & Exhibitionem Corporis & Sanguinis Christi docere Reformatos, sed & Sacramentalem, licèt non Corporalem, utpote in neutra Confessione Augustana, nec in priori magis, quàm posteriori, edoctam.
english: Answer. First, they can do the same with the Invariata's words: while it says Christ's body and blood are truly present and distributed, they may take that as only spiritual presence and distribution.

Second, even confessors of the Invariata alone do not deny spiritual presence and distribution any more than spiritual exhibition and eating — especially since they also insist that their own corporal presence, distribution, eating, and exhibition are nonetheless hyperphysical and supernatural.

Third, the Reformed do not teach a naked spiritual presence, distribution, and exhibition of Christ's body and blood, but a sacramental one as well — though not a corporal one, which neither Augsburg Confession teaches, earlier or later.

source_text:
§. IX.
Dorschei Canones reliqui, quibus Confessionem Philippicam, privata tantum Auctoritate, non etiam publica Subsequente factam, quin, publicâ Auctoritate improbatam rejectamque, esse, innuit,
english: §. IX. Dorsche's remaining canons hint that the Philippica Confession rested on private authority alone — not on later public authority — and was even condemned and rejected by public authority.

source_text: praeterquam quòd, ab Auctoribus supra allegatis, sigillatim Joh. Crocio Comm. Cap. LVI. pag. 746. ab ipso etiam Mentzero Lutherano, non agnoscuntur,
english: Besides, the authors already cited do not own those canons — least of all John Crocius (Commentary, ch. 56, p. 746), and not even Mentzer the Lutheran.

source_text: ita ex ipso Dorscheo falsitatis arguuntur, per jam tum retrò memoratarum ad Ferdinandum I. Imperatorem, à Statibus Imperii datarum & a Dorscheo pagina 20. integra in vernacula nostra lingua recensitarum literarum, verba sequentia:
english: So Dorsche himself convicts them of falsehood: the letter already named — from the Imperial Estates to Emperor Ferdinand I — which he prints in full in our vernacular at page 20, runs as follows:

source_text: Gleichergestalt wollen wir auch hiemit die Apologi/ so durch unsere Vorfahren/ und zum theil uns /auf gemeltem Reichs Tag zu Augspurg/ überreichet / aber man nicht hat annehmen wollen/wie die selbige hernach zu Wittenberg gedruckt/und auf gedachtem Colloquio zu Wormbs A. 1540. neben obberührten verbesserten Confession übergeben / ausdrucklich repetirt und uns darzu bekennt haben.
english: Likewise we hereby also hold the Apology which our ancestors — and partly we ourselves — presented at that Augsburg Diet, though it was not accepted; afterward it was printed at Wittenberg, and at the Worms Colloquy in 1540 it was delivered beside the improved Confession already named — expressly repeated, and we have confessed ourselves to it.

source_text: Wie denn auch gleicher gestalt unsere Meinung dahin gericht / daß wir andere der unsere Schrifften und repetirte Confessionen/ so der Kays: Maj. aufgehaltenen Reichs-Tagen und Colloquien/durch die Ständ/unserer Religion/zu weiterer Erklärung der beständigen und unwiederlegten Warheit / und Abwendung deren eine lange Zeit eingerissenen falschen Lehren und Mißbrauchen übergeben / und zum Theil publiciret/ hiemit nicht verwerffen / noch begeben / sondern dieselbe/im Verstand der heiligen Schrifft und ieko erneurter Augspurgischen Confession und Apologi gemäß/in alle Weg wollen vorbehalten haben. Da auch unser Gegentheil etliche Articul oder Wörter in dieser Augspurgischen Confession und Apologi / welche zum Anfang dieser hochnothwendigen / unvermeidentlichen Veränderung / zum Theil/ auch nach Art und Gebrauch der Teutschen Sprachen zu reden / zum glimpfligsten gestellt / und sonderlich da vom H. Sacrament und Messe / auch von der Römischen Kirchen gemelt wird / zu ihrem Vortheil und dahin deuten oder ziehen wolten / als wenn wir auch mit ihren abgöttischen Lehren und Ceremonien/in denen sich gleichwol nachgehends allerhand Christliche Aenderungen zugetragen / der Päpstischen Kirchen /und sonderlich dem Greuel der transubstantiation , der Päpstischen Meß / und was dem anhängig / einig/ so erklären wir uns hiemit abermal / daß es die Meinung gar nicht hat / &c.
english: In the same way our mind is this: we do not reject or give up our other writings and repeated Confessions — those the Estates of our religion handed in at Imperial Diets and colloquies under His Majesty, partly published, to explain the standing, unrefuted truth and to drive out long-settled false teaching and abuse.
We mean to keep them in every way in the sense of holy Scripture and of the now-renewed Augsburg Confession and Apology.

And when our opponents twist some early, mild articles or words in that Confession and Apology — set gently, partly in German speech-habit, especially where the holy Sacrament, the Mass, and the Roman Church are named — as if we agreed with their idolatrous papal teachings and ceremonies (in which Christian changes later came anyway), and above all with the horror of transubstantiation, the papal Mass, and what hangs on it: we declare again that this is not our meaning at all.

source_text: & post. Hinwiderum aber ist unser Meinung und Fürsatz gar nicht/ daß wir in unsern Landen/ Gebieten / Kirchen / und Schulen einige andere Lehr / denn die / wie obgemelt/ in der heiligen göttlichen Schrifft gegründet/und der Augspurgischen Confession und Apologi in ihrem rechten Verstand gemäß / dulden oder vertheidigen/ sondern uns allein zu der erkanten Warheit bekennen/ und nichts / so derselben entgegen/ einreissen lassen / oder gestatten wollen. &c. Confer. Historiam Conventus Nauenburgici hôc ipso anno in vernacula nostra denuo recensitam a Dn. D. Hönnio, Consiliario Saxonico Ducali ac Secretario intimo pag. 103. 105. 106. 107.
english: And afterward: on the contrary, it is not our mind or purpose to tolerate or defend in our lands, territories, churches, and schools any teaching other than what is grounded, as said above, in holy Scripture and fits the Augsburg Confession and Apology in their right sense.
We mean to confess the known truth alone, and to let nothing against it break in or be allowed.
Compare the History of the Naumburg Convention, reviewed again this very year in our vernacular by Dr. Hoennius, Ducal Saxon councillor and intimate secretary (pp. 103, 105, 106, 107).

source_text:
J. X.
Quae hactenus pro Variata seu Philippica Confessione Augustana disputavimus, non in Reformatorum gratiam disputata fuisse quivis facile intelligat, utpote quibus Invariata Confessio non minus grata, atque Variata est, id quod vel ex solo Colloquio Lipsiaco, superiori seculo Saxonicos inter, Brandenb. & Hassiacos Theologos, habito, satis superque constat, nisi quod cum Joh. Museo ex Martino Chemnitio, de posteriori teneant, plerosque Articulos in ea fusius deductos & uberius declaratos esse, multa etiam utilia in ista editione reperiri.
english: J. X. Anyone can see that what we have argued so far for the Variata or Philippica Augsburg Confession was not argued to favor the Reformed.
To them the Invariata is no less welcome than the Variata — clear enough from the Leipzig Colloquy alone in the last century among Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian theologians.
With John Museus, following Martin Chemnitz, they only add that in the later edition most articles are drawn out more fully and stated more richly, and that many useful things appear there.

source_text: Disputata interim sunt partim in gratiam Philippicae famae, quam perinde atque Lutheri, in deliciis habent Reformati, omnibus Reformatoribus Pontificiae Idolomaniae hanc gratiam deberi augurati, ne Scripta Factaque istorum vel temere suggillentur, vel exagitentur odiose haereseosque coarguantur;
english: Meantime the case was argued partly for Philippica fame, which the Reformed cherish as they do Luther's.
They reckon that favor owed to every Reformer who broke with papal idol-madness: do not rashly sneer at their writings and deeds, nor bait them as heretics.

source_text: Partim in gratiam Augustanae Confessionis cujuscunque, ne a Pontificiis [quod ut saepe factum, ita hodieque fit] alterationis hujusmodi infimuletur, ob quam Protestantes Pace Religiosa indigni ab Imperatore Augusto aliisque Statibusque Imperii Pontificiis, censeri debeant;
english: Partly it was for the Augsburg Confession in either form: so the papal side — as they often have, and still do — cannot charge this kind of alteration, and then say Protestants deserve to lose the Religious Peace before the Emperor and the other papal Estates of the Empire.

source_text: Partim in gratiam Invariatae Confessionis in specie, hancque solam & cum oppressione ac exterminio Variatae, amplectentium, ne, dum nimis superstitiose verbis prioris inhaerere satagunt, ad phrasin Pontificiam de praesentia Corporis & Sanguinis Christi in Coena sub Speciebus panis & vini, hujusque phraseos sensum, eo tempore, quo Confessio edebatur, Occidentali Ecclesiae unice receptum, adigantur, id quod metuendum fuisse jam olim innuere Status Imperii, Naunburgi Anno 61. congregati, in praefatione sua, Augustanae Confessioni Invariatae praemissa & Ferdinando Imperatori inscripta;
english: Partly it was for the Invariata in particular — and for those who hug that form alone while crushing and wiping out the Variata.

If they cling too superstitiously to the earlier wording, they can be pushed into the papal phrase about Christ's Body and Blood present in the Supper under the species of bread and wine, in the sense the Western Church alone then held when the Confession was issued.
The Imperial Estates at Naumburg in 1561 already flagged that danger in the preface they set before the Invariata and addressed to Emperor Ferdinand.

source_text: Vel dum ab hoc sensu recedunt, & obscuriorem, certe Pontificiis Doctoribus & Statibus Imperii plerisque isto tempore ignotum, sequuntur, a Dorscheo cit. loc. pag. 183. in fine traditum, aequivocationis, Jesuiticis haud absimilis, rei inveniantur, ab illis alias haud raro, etsi satis perperam, Reformatis impingi solitae.
english: Or when they leave that sense and take an obscurer one — one most papal doctors and Imperial Estates then did not know — Dorsche at the place cited (p. 183, end) still leaves them open to a charge of equivocation not unlike Jesuit practice.
Papal writers elsewhere often pin that charge on the Reformed, though quite wrongly.

source_text: Praeterea, ne ab Hoffmanno Helmstadiensi aliisque Lutheranis Theologis, jure urgeantur, Formulae Concordiae spurium Augustanae Confessionis Exemplar insertum esse; vide Hoffmanni Apologiam ad D. Olearium & Paulum Nicandrum, pag. 691. citatam Auctori des Anhangs der ausführlichen Behauptung pag. 29. & feqq.
english: Besides, so Hoffmann of Helmstedt and other Lutheran theologians cannot rightly press that the Formula of Concord slipped in a spurious Augsburg Confession exemplar.
See Hoffmann's Apology to Dr. Olearius and Paul Nicander (p. 691), cited by the author of the Appendix to the Ausführliche Behauptung (pp. 29ff.).

source_text: Partim denique & maxime omnium in gratiam & Veritatis & Pacis Protestanticae, ne, quemadmodum Evangelicorum utraque pars in re & substantia Veritatis, quoad Articulum de Sacra Coena, consentit, (id quod infra ad oculum patebit) ita litigiis de verbis, in alterutra Confessione Augustana repertis, distrahantur & inter tripudia Pontificia mordeant se mutuo, a se mutuo consumendi.
english: Finally — and most of all — it was for Truth and for Protestant peace.
Both Evangelical sides already agree in the matter and substance of the truth on the article of the Lord's Supper (that will be plain below).
They must not be torn apart by fights over words in either Augsburg Confession, and bite one another to pieces while Rome dances.

source_text:
§. XI.
Disputationem nostram pro Confessione Variata non impugnanda aut rejicienda institutam, claudimus paulò ante allegato judicio D. MARTINI CHEMNITII de Controversiis quae superiori tempore, circa quosdam August. Confess. Articulos, motae & agitatae sunt, & tam à D. Polycarpo Lysero Anno 1594. Wittenbergae, quam à D. Bajero Anno 1676. Jenae, edito, ab utroque etiam laudato, quin novissimè à Wittenbergensi Theologo, D. Hannekenio, exasciato dicto, Declarat. Theol. de vera August. Conf. Estimatione Quaest. Prelim. 4. sub finem. pag. 6. cujus Judicii Chemniziani verba ita habent:
english: §. XI. We close this defense of the Variata — that it is not to be attacked or thrown out — with the Chemnitz judgment already cited a little above.
It is the piece On the Controversies once stirred about certain Augsburg Confession articles, edited by Polycarp Leyser at Wittenberg in 1594 and again by Bajer at Jena in 1676, praised by both.

Most recently the Wittenberg theologian Hannekenius smoothed the same saying in his Theological Declaration on the true Estimation of the Augsburg Confession (Preliminary Question 4, near the end, p. 6).
Chemnitz's words are these:

source_text: Nec video, quomodo rectè & utiliter possit rejici & damnari Editio Anni 42. Cùm enim ad Annum 42. institutum fuisset Colloquium Hagonoënse & judicaretur, utile fore, ut Corpus & Forma Doctrinae nostrarum Ecclesiarum proponeretur, tanquam materia Colloquii, edita est illo anno Wittenbergae, additâ alicubi pleniori declaratione.
english: "I do not see how the edition of 1542 can rightly or usefully be rejected and condemned.
When the Hagenau colloquy was set for that year, it seemed useful to put forward the body and form of our churches' doctrine as the colloquy's matter.
So that year Wittenberg printed the edition, with a fuller declaration added in places."

source_text: Illa Editio eodem anno, nomine Confessionis Augustanae, proposita est Wormatiae; eandem Editionem in Colloquio Ratisbonensi, ut formam Doctrinae nostrarum Ecclesiarum, opposuerunt adversariis. Et factum illud fuit de Consilio, Lutheri approbatione & Consensu.
english: "That same year the edition was laid on the table at Worms under the name of the Augsburg Confession.
At the Regensburg colloquy they set the same edition against their adversaries as the form of our churches' doctrine.
And that was done by counsel — with Luther's approval and consent."

source_text: Ita ab Anno 46. & postea in omnibus Comitiis & Actionibus de Religione ad hanc Editionem se nostri contulerunt, quam vocarunt Confessionem Augustanam. Nec potest demonstrari, quod aliquid sit vel errorum, vel depravationum in illis declarationibus, quae in Editione Anno 42. accesserunt, exceptâ mutilatione in X. Articulo.
english: "So from 1546 on, in every diet and religious proceeding, our side kept turning to this edition — and they called it the Augsburg Confession.
No one can show errors or corruptions in the declarations added in the 1542 edition, save the mutilation in Article X."

source_text: Imò Cochlaeus Wormatiae Anno 40. & Pighius Anno 41. Ratisbonae graviter tulerunt, multis Articulis pleniori declaratione, plurimùm lucis accessisse. Unde videbant veras sententias magis illustrari & Thaidis Babylonicae turpitudinem manifestius denudari, & maluissent isti simpliciter retineri editionem Anni 31. sicut scripta ipsorum testantur.
english: "Indeed Cochlaeus at Worms in 1540, and Pighius at Regensburg in 1541, took it hard that a fuller declaration on many articles let in so much light.
They saw true opinions set out more clearly, and the shame of Babylon's Thais stripped plainer still.
They would rather have kept the 1531 edition alone — their own writings say so."

source_text: Cùm verò Editio Anni 40. omnium manibus versetur, & plerisque ignota & vix unquam visa fuerit prima Editio Anni 31. nec aliquid falsi contineat, sed tantùm necessarias quasdam Declarationes, nescio, quomodo possit omninò vel simpliciter rejici & damnari sine perturbatione Ecclesiarum. Hucusque Chemnitius.
english: "But the 1540 edition is in everyone's hands, while the first edition of 1531 is unknown to most and scarcely ever seen.
It contains nothing false — only some needed declarations.
I do not see how it can be thrown out altogether, or simply condemned, without disturbing the churches."
Thus far Chemnitz.

source_text:
§. XII.
Adhuc Annotationis nostrae primae MEMBRUM PRIMUM expedivimus, ipsius Augustanae Confessionis Naturam concernens; sequitur, ut ad MEMBRUM SECUNDUM delati, de Confessionis ejusdem Theologis & Sociis promiscuè, pro instituti nostri ratione, paucis agamus. Ubi omnium primò distinguendum arbitramur, inter Latè & Strictè sic appellandos.
english: §. XII. So far we have finished the first member of this first Annotation — the nature of the Augsburg Confession itself.
Next, under the second member, we treat briefly, as our plan requires, of that Confession's theologians and associates in the broad sense.
First we distinguish those so called loosely from those so called strictly.

source_text: Ad prius genus referimus, quotquot, etiam extra fines Germaniae constituti, vel (1) totam Augustanam Confessionem approbant eique subscribere parati sunt (quales olim fuerunt Bucerus & Calvinus, de quorum priori passim Chytraeus Hist. sua pag. 651. & 656. 659.; de posteriori Auctor der ausführlicher Behauptung 20. peculiari disquisitione: Ob Herr Joh. Calvinus seeliger für einen Augspurgischen Confessions-Verwandten zu seiner Zeit sey gehalten worden/ oder nicht? a pag. 72. ad 90. Adde Pareum in Irenico pag. 293.);
english: Under the looser class we put all who, even outside Germany, either (1) approve the whole Augsburg Confession and stand ready to subscribe — as Bucer and Calvin once did.

On Bucer see Chytraeus's History at pp. 651, 656, and 659; on Calvin, the Author of the ausführlicher Behauptung 20, in the special inquiry whether the late John Calvin was counted an Augsburg Confession kinsman in his day (pp. 72–90); add Pareus, Irenicum, p. 293.

source_text: Vel (2.) plerisque saltem dictae Confessionis, sincero animo adstipulantur, licèt ob duriorem unam vel alteram Articuli, maximè decimi, phrasin haud omnino admissam, nec amplexi Confessionem in totum sint, nec ei subscripserint, à Subscriptione vel semet abstinentes ipsos, vel ab aliis prohibiti: Quales Tetrapolitani vulgò dicti, Argentinenses, Memmingenses, Constantienses & Lindavienses, Zwinglii Dogma de S. Coena olim secuti, exhibitâ ob id peculiari in Comitiis Augustanis, Confessione, una tamen, cum Augustana, à Caesare rejicienda. Chytr. pag. 678. 679. Renuisse hos subscribere Augustanae Confessioni, ostendunt passim Nostrates, Pareus, Georgius Pauli, &c. aliis interim e Chytraeo Historia, pag. 130. sustinentibus, eos à subscribendo, ex Statuum Protestanticorum sententia, per plura saltem, coercitos fuisse.
english: Or (2) they sincerely agree with most of the Confession, yet because of a harder phrasing in one article or another — above all the tenth — they have neither taken the whole Confession nor subscribed, whether by their own abstention or because others barred them.

Such were the so-called Tetrapolitans of Strasbourg, Memmingen, Constance, and Lindau, who once followed Zwingli on the Supper and therefore presented their own Confession at the Augsburg Diet, which the Emperor meant to reject together with the Augsburg.

Chytraeus, pp. 678–679. Our writers (Pareus, Georg Pauli, and others) show that they refused subscription; others, citing Chytraeus's History p. 130, hold that the Protestant Estates' judgment at least partly forced them not to subscribe.

source_text: (3.) Ne illi quidem, latiori hûc sensu, Theologorum Sociorumque Augustanae Confessionis nomine, omnino indigni aestimandi, qui pro locorum temporumque circumstantiis, in hoc, vel isto Regno ac Principatu, August. Confess., utcunque, quà Substantiam, verbo Dei congruam à se habitam, multorum tamen malorum facem, per accidens saltem, futuram veriti, subscriptioni ejusdem semet subduxerunt: Quale quid Theod. Beza & Pet. Martyr, in Colloquio Possiaceno in Gallia fecisse feruntur. Videatur Pareus Iren. pag. 294. 295. Joh. Crocius, Comment in August. Conf. pag. 144. & seqq.
english: (3) Even those who, for local and temporal reasons, withdrew from subscription are not wholly unworthy of the wider name of Augsburg Confession theologians and associates.
They held the Confession congruent with God's word as to substance, yet feared it would become — at least by accident — a torch of many evils in this or that kingdom or principality.
Beza and Peter Martyr are said to have done this at the Colloquy of Poissy in France. See Pareus, Irenicum, pp. 294–295; Crocius on the Augsburg Confession, p. 144ff.

source_text: Ratio Assertionis nostrae haec est, quòd, ex una parte, qui Confessionem aliquam approbant, illi se eidem associasse animo, intelliguntur; ex altera verò parte, per ipsam Christianae alicujus Confessionis Christianorumque Confitentium Naturam, nemo non hujusmodi Confessioni consentiens, ejusdem socius reputari consuevit.
english: Our reason is twofold.
Those who approve a confession are understood to have joined themselves to it in mind.
And by the very nature of a Christian confession and of Christians who confess, everyone who consents to it is customarily counted its associate.

source_text: Ad posterius verò genus pertinent, primariò quidem ac immediatè, vel potiùs primò quà ordinem & prioritatem temporis, Imperii Romano-Germanici STATUS OMNES, quorum nomine Confessio August. confecta atque exhibita est, quique eandem manibus suis subscripserunt, unà cum Theologis, Confessionem illam vel adornantibus, vel operam suam quamcunque ad ejus adornationem conferentibus; secundario & mediatè dictorum Imperii Statuum, aliorum quoque, horum exemplum secutorum, Successores universi cum suis Theologis, in hanc usque diem, August. Confess. vel Invariatam solam, vel solam Variatam, vel utramque, ceu re ac Substantia Veritatis unam eandemque, defendentibus, Lutheranorum, sive Reformatorum proprio veniant nomine, communi aliàs Protestantium seu Evangelicorum & γνησίως Catholicorum appellatione, Pontificiis, seu Papam infallibile Universae Ecclesiae caput, summam tàm in Temporalibus, quàm in Spiritualibus tenens potestatem, agnoscentibus, contradistinguendi; sive Articulum Augustanae Confessionis X., de Spirituali & Sacramentali tantum praesentia & exhibitione Corporis & Sanguinis Christi, sive (quod tamen nullibi Augustana Confessio expressit) etiam de Corporali interpretentur:
english: Under the stricter class fall, primarily and immediately — or rather first in time — all the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation in whose name the Augsburg Confession was framed and exhibited, and who subscribed it with their own hands, together with the theologians who drafted it or helped in any way.

Secondarily and mediately come all successors of those Estates (and of others who followed their example), with their theologians to this day, who defend the Augsburg Confession — the Invariata alone, the Variata alone, or both as one and the same in the substance of truth — whether under the name Lutheran or Reformed.

They are set apart, under the common name of Protestants or Evangelicals and genuinely Catholic, from the papal party that owns the Pope as infallible head of the universal church with supreme temporal and spiritual power.

It does not matter whether they read Article X of a spiritual and sacramental presence and exhibition only of Christ's body and blood, or even of a corporal presence (which the Augsburg Confession nowhere states).

source_text: Nam istos non minus, atque hos, August. Confess. Socios habitos semper fuisse (1.) exemplo FRIDERICI PALATINI in Conventu Naumburgico Anno 1561. & Comitiis Augustanis Anno 1566. constat; qua de re prolixius Auctor der ausführlichen Behauptung in Append. a p. 36. ad 43. Pareus in Iren. p. m. 292. & 297. Joh. Crocius in tractatu Germanico nuncupato: Summarische Nachricht und beweißliche Anzeig: Daß die im deutschen Land der Reformirten Religion zugethane Stände und Kirchen/als Mitgenossen der Augspurgischen Confession, des Religions-Friedens fähig seyn/ à num. 123. ad 130. à pag. 54. ad 58. itemque in Comment. de August. Confess. Societate, Questione 2. Cap. XVIII. & Cap. XXI. nec non Dn. D. Becmannus noster l. c. pag. 99. & seqq. (2.) exemplo PHILIPPI, HASSIAE LANDGRAVII, istorum, i.e. Reformatorum partibus constanter faventis, & rigidiores, voce pariter ac scriptis Literis plurimis, in easdem partes, magno cum zelo sollicitantis ac inducentis, apud Chytraeum in Actis cum Zwinglianis, Histor. à pag. 633. & seqq. & apud Calixtum de Tolerantia Reformatorum n. 62. Batavica, & n. 65. novissima Helmst. Edit. nec non in Historia A. C. trium Theologorum germanicè conscripta & a Chemnitii genero in Lat. translata.
english: That the Reformed no less than the Lutherans have always been held Augsburg Confession associates appears (1) from Frederick the Palatine at Naumburg in 1561 and at the Augsburg Diet in 1566.

See more fully the Author of the ausführlichen Behauptung, Appendix pp. 36–43; Pareus, Irenicum, pp. 292 and 297; Crocius's German Summarische Nachricht… (nos. 123–130; pp. 54–58), and his Comment on Augsburg Confession Society, Q.2, caps. XVIII and XXI; also our Becmann, loc. cit., p. 99ff.

(2) From Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, who steadily favored the Reformed side and with great zeal pressed the more rigid into it by speech and many letters — in Chytraeus's Acts with the Zwinglians from p. 633ff.; Calixtus, On Tolerance of the Reformed, n. 62 (Batavian) and n. 65 (newest Helmstedt); and the History of the A.C. by three theologians, written in German and Latinized by Chemnitz's son-in-law.

source_text: Atque sic per consequens, August. Confess. Socii quoque indubii sunt Marchiones & Electores Brandenburgici, à GEORGII, Marchionis ac Confess. August. Subsignatoris, & JOACHIMI SECUNDI, Electoris Brandenburgici, & Confessionis Augustanae in regiones suas Introductoris usque tempore, non obstante; quod DIVUS JOHANNES SIGISMUNDUS gloriosissimae memoriae, AUGUSTISSIMI REGIS NOSTRI Proavus, cum Successoribus suis inque omne aevum, per Dei gratiam, secuturis olim, Friderici Palatini interpretationem August. Confess. quoad Articulum X., unà cum Theologis suis non impugnaverit;
english: Consequently the Brandenburg Margraves and Electors are likewise undoubted Augsburg Confession associates — from George (Margrave and AC subscriber) and Joachim II (Elector who brought the Confession into his lands) down to our day.

That holds even though blessed Johann Sigismund of glorious memory — great-grandfather of our most august King — with his successors forever after, by God's grace, did not attack Frederick the Palatine's reading of AC Art. X, nor did his theologians.

source_text: Cùm ceterà, tàm ipse Joh. Sigismundus, quàm ejus Successores, tum semetipsos Declarationibus variis, tùm Theologos suos, per Statuta etiam Facultatis Theologicae Francofurtensis, solenni juramento, ad August. Conf. Carolo V. Anno 1530. exhibitam, ac deinceps prolixius expositam, ceu ad praecipuum Regionum Brandenburgicarum Librum Symbolicum, seriò severéque obligaverint, totóque pectore addixerint. Vid. Joh. Crocium Comment. de A. C. Societate parte 1. integra, à pag. 1. ad 30.;
english: For the rest, Johann Sigismund and his successors have bound themselves by various declarations, and their theologians through the Frankfurt theological faculty statutes, by solemn oath, to the Augsburg Confession shown to Charles V in 1530 and later more fully set out — as the chief symbolic book of the Brandenburg lands — and have devoted themselves to it with their whole heart.
See Crocius, Comment on A.C. Society, part 1 entire, pp. 1–30.

source_text: Ut hinc etiam Lutheranae Ecclesiae haud incelebris hodieque Antecessor Consistoriiique S. Sambiensis Regiomonti Borussorum Assessor, nunc etiam quartus in ordine, Theologiae Professor Ordinar. Christianus Waltherus, de Facultatis nostrae Juramento certior factus, quô post Sacram. Scripturam, solis quatuor Conciliis Oecumenicis & Augustanae Confessioni ceu Symbolicis Scriptis perpetuò nos adhaesuros, solenniter recipimus, abhinc annis duobus, Theologiae Doctoris Gradum à Facultate nostra Theologica petere nullus dubitaverit, etiam eôdem, post praestitum subsignatumque Juramentum, jussu PIENTISSIMI REGIS NOSTRI, à dicta Facultate, per me, eo tempore Decanum, mactatus sit, prout fusius id refert Significatio, nomine Facultatis Theologicae Viadrinae, Anno 1702. typis evulgata. Tam Juramentum Facultatis nostrae, quam Mandatum Regium, utpote clementissimum, & Promovendi pariter Lutherani, atque Promoventium Reformatorum conatibus faventissime applaudens, non abs re fuerit, hôc locô subjunxisse. Juramentum hisce conceptum verbis est &c.
english: Hence also Christian Walther — still a well-known Lutheran churchman, Assessor of the Holy Sambian Consistory at Königsberg in Prussia, and now fourth Ordinary Professor of Theology — once informed of our faculty oath (that after Holy Scripture we solemnly bind ourselves forever to the four ecumenical councils alone and to the Augsburg Confession as symbolic writings) did not hesitate two years ago to seek a doctorate of theology from our faculty.

After he took and signed the oath, by command of our most pious King the faculty decorated him through me (then Dean), as the 1702 printed Signification in the Viadrina theological faculty's name reports more fully.

It is not out of place here to add both our faculty oath and the royal mandate — most gracious, and warmly favoring the efforts of the Lutheran candidate and of the Reformed promoters alike. The oath runs in these words, &c.

source_text: Ego Magister Christianus Walther juro, me sanam Doctrinam Evangelii Christi & verbi Prophetarum & Apostolorum, cujus capita in tribus Symbolis & Confessione, Carolo V. Augustae exhibita, comprehensa & explicata habentur, ut rectè cognitam ita diligenter & fideliter custoditam traditurum ac defensurum; Omnia falsa, Heretica & cum manifesto Dei verbo pugnantia, tam veterum quàm novorum Arrianorum, & aliorum Fanaticorum hominum Dogmata sedulò ac pro virili declinaturum impugnaturumque esse:
english: I, Master Christian Walther, swear that I will hand on and defend the sound doctrine of Christ's Gospel and of the Prophets' and Apostles' word — whose chief points are contained and explained in the three Symbols and in the Confession shown to Charles V at Augsburg — knowing it rightly and keeping it diligently and faithfully.
I will carefully and as far as I can refuse and attack all false and heretical dogmas that fight the clear word of God, whether of old or new Arians or of other fanatics.

source_text:
De iis, qui ad gradus Theologicos sunt admittendi, severè judicaturum & graviter pronunciaturum, hunc Gradum nullibi repetiturum & omnia quae ad Ecclesiae Dei utilitatem, ad Gloriam Christi, & ad hanc Facultatem atque Scholam juvandam, ornandam atque augendam, videbuntur spectare, summa fide & perpetuo studio facturum esse; Sic me Deus adjuvet per sanctum suum Verbum.
Juramentum suprà scriptum me fideliter servaturum, tam nominis mei subscriptione, quàm appresso Sigillo meo sancte attestor atque polliceor, d. 15. Aprilis Anno 1702.
(L. S.)
M. Christianus Walther,
Pastor Sackheimensis, Consistorii Sambiensis Assessor, & Societatis Scientiarum Brandenburgicae membrum, manu suâ.
english: As to those admitted to theological degrees, I will judge strictly and speak with weight; I will not take this degree over again elsewhere; and with highest faithfulness and constant zeal I will do whatever seems to serve God's church, Christ's glory, and the help, honor, and growth of this faculty and school. So help me God through His holy Word.
I holy attest and promise that I will keep the oath written above, both by signing my name and by affixing my seal, 15 April 1702.
(L.S.) M. Christian Walther, Pastor of Sackheim, Assessor of the Sambian Consistory, and member of the Brandenburg Society of Sciences — in his own hand.

source_text:
Rescriptum vero Regium ita sonat:
FRIDERICUS, D. G. REX BORUSSIAE,
Marchio Brandenburgensis, S. R. J. ArchiCamerarius & Princeps Elector, Magdeburgi, Cliviae, Juliae, Montium, Stetini, Pomeraniae &c. Dux &c.
Reverendi, Doctissimi, Dilecti ac Fideles;
Etsi jam antehac perspecta nobis sit M. Christiani Waltheri, Pastoris Sackheimensis Regiomonti Borussorum, haud vulgaribus elogiis à vobis commendati, singularis Eruditio, morum probitas juxta & vitae integritas, Nosque de meritis ejus affatim edoctissimi, adeò, ut vel ex hac sola ratione, illum exoptatis honoribus neutiquam destitutum censeamus; Magis tamen nos incitavit, ut votis ipsius, vestrisque humillimis annueremus precibus, rarissimum hactenus Theologi Lutherani exemplum, Docturam Theologicam à Reformatae fidei Doctoribus non minori fiducia expetentis, quàm horum in promovendis ejus desideriis est promptitudo & reciprocum studium. Non potest non Nobis hoc esse gratissimum, cùm salutaria quaevis ac prospera Rei, tàm Publicae, quàm Ecclesiasticae, inde ominari liceat. Consentimus itaque non solùm, verùm mandamus etiam Tibi, Samueli Strimesio, Facultatis Theologicae Decano, nec non Doctori & Professori Ordinario, ut & Pastori Ecclesiae Primario, ut praefatum M. Christianum Waltherum, nunc quidem in Facultate Vestra, S. S. Theologiae Doctorem declares, in proximo verò Promotionis publicae futuro Actu, talem publicè proclames & renuncies, omniumque Privilegiorum ac Jurium, summo huic Axiomati annexorum, ac Doctoribus Theologiae per S. R. J. competentium, participem reddas, quod Divinum Numen secundare dignetur. valete, de Gratia Nostra Regia securi. Dabantur Coloniae ad Svevum d. 20. Martii. Ao. 1702.

FRIDERICUS REX.

PAULUS, LIB. BARO de FUCHS.
Ad Facultatem Theologicam Universitatis Viadrinae.
english: The royal rescript runs thus: Frederick, by God's grace King of Prussia, Margrave of Brandenburg, Arch-Chamberlain of the Holy Roman Empire and Prince Elector, Duke of Magdeburg, Cleves, Julich, Berg, Stettin, Pomerania, and so on.

Reverend, most learned, beloved and faithful: Walther's uncommon learning, upright manners, and integrity of life — praised by you without ordinary compliments — were already clear to us, and we know his merits well enough that on that ground alone we would not leave him without the honors he seeks.

What moved us still more to grant his wish and your humble petitions is this rare case: a Lutheran theologian seeking a theological doctorate from Reformed doctors with as much confidence as they show readiness and mutual zeal in advancing his desire.

That can only please us, since every wholesome good for the commonwealth and the church may be hoped from it. We therefore not only consent but command you, Samuel Strimesius — dean of the theological faculty, ordinary doctor and professor, and primary pastor — to declare M. Christian Walther now Doctor of Sacred Theology in your faculty, and at the next public promotion to proclaim him such, and to admit him to all privileges and rights belonging to that highest title and to doctors of theology in the Holy Roman Empire — which may God favor. Farewell, secure of our royal grace. Given at Cologne on the Spree, 20 March 1702.
Frederick the King. Paul, Freiherr von Fuchs. To the Theological Faculty of the Viadrina University.

source_text:
§. XIII.
Ope Distinctionis, superiori §.XII traditae, in facili est decidere, & vel justè, vel nefariè, decisam deprehendere Quaestionum Theologico-Historicarum bigam: Utrum Reformati Augustanae Confessionis Socii? &, Utrum Pacis Religiosae participes iidem habendi?
english: §. XIII. With the distinction given in §.XII above, it is easy to settle — and to see whether the settlement was just or wicked — this pair of theological-historical questions:
Are the Reformed associates of the Augsburg Confession? And are they to be counted participants in the Religious Peace?

source_text: Utriusque, cumprimis posterioris, affirmativam veram & prioris Veritatem necessariò supponentem inferentemque, prolixius evicerunt Joh. Crocius, Tractatu Germanico suprâ allegato, & Commentario suo spissiori, quaestione secunda, Auctor item der ausführlichen Behauptung à pag. 90. ad 111., Georgius Pauli in Reformato Augustano, & Venerandus Facultatis nostrae Senior contra Liebhardum cap. 4. & sexto integris, inter alias probationes, maximè ex Comitio Anni 1566. Augustano (de quo prolixissimè Joh. Crocius cit. Comment. Cap. 18.) Cap. 4. §. 8. pag. 102.;
english: On both questions — especially the second, which must presuppose and imply the first — the affirmative is true.

Joh. Crocius proved it at length in the German tract already cited and in his denser Commentary, question 2; so did the author of the Ausführliche Behauptung, pp. 90–111; Georgius Pauli in the Reformatus Augustanus; and the venerable Senior of our faculty against Liebhard in chapters 4 and 6 entire.
Among other proofs they lean chiefly on the Augsburg Diet of 1566 (treated most fully by Crocius, Comm. Cap. 18), Cap. 4 §.8 p. 102;

source_text: Praetereà Cap. 6. §. 8., Articuli VII. Instrumenti Pacis ut notatu dignissima ita celebratissima verba adducens, quibus Reformati disertè Augustanae Confessionis Sociis annumerantur, omniaque inimica & Achristianô exemplo, Sanguinem Christianum sitientia temerè tumultuantium nonnullorum Theologorum acerborum molimina, ictu unô prosternuntur. Verba Instrumenti Pacifici ita habent: Unanimi quoque Caesareae Majestatis omniumque Imperii Ordinum Consensu placuit, ut quicquid Juris aut beneficii, cum omnes aliae Constitutiones Imperii, tùm Pax Religionis & Publica haec Transactio in eaque decisio gravaminum, caeteris Catholicis & Augustanae Confessionis addictis Statibus & Subditis tribuunt, id etiam iis, qui inter eos Reformati vocantur, competere debeat.
english: Further, Cap. 6 §.8 cites the famous words of Article VII of the Peace Instrument — worth noting, and celebrated — by which the Reformed are expressly counted among Augsburg Confession associates.
With that one stroke fall the hostile schemes of certain harsh theologians who, in an un-Christian way, rashly riot as if thirsting for Christian blood.

The Peace Instrument's words run: By unanimous consent of the Imperial Majesty and of all Estates of the Empire it was resolved that whatever right or benefit the other constitutions of the Empire, the Religious Peace, and this public settlement (with its decision of grievances) grant to other Catholic and Augsburg-Confession states and subjects, that same must also belong to those among them called Reformed.

source_text: Verba haec, contra verè pedanticos Criticos, egregiè vindicavit nuperrimus Auctor der gründliche Vorstellung/ welche das einige wahre Mittel zur Vereinigung der beyden Evangelischen Religionen in Deutschland sey/ pag. 11. 9.8. nobis alibi, in ingenua scilicet in Arminianismus Inquisitione nostra, pag. 302. citatus laudatusque.
english: Against truly pedantic critics, the newest author of the Gründliche Vorstellung (Which Is the One True Means for Uniting the Two Evangelical Religions in Germany) has finely defended these words at pp. 11 and 98.
We cited and praised that author elsewhere — namely in our Ingenua in Arminianismus Inquisitio, p. 302.

source_text: Neque hîc sibi ipsis infesti sunt Reformati, quando cum Neostadianis Theologis Cap. IV. à pag. 143. de Augustana Confessione, contra hos, qui eam, tantum non Sacrae Scripturae aequiparatum eunt, annotant (id quod Calovius, iniquè profectò & non nisi per convitium, Calviniana convitia interpretatur, Crit. Sacr. pag. 68.) Esse eam scriptam annis non ita multis post Reformationis initium, in quo non tam subitò potuerunt omnia perspici & explicari &c. &c.
english: Nor are the Reformed here their own enemies when, with the Neustadt theologians (Cap. IV from p. 143) on the Augsburg Confession, they note against those who nearly equate it with Holy Scripture — which Calovius unfairly, and only by insult, reads as "Calvinian insults" (Crit. Sacr. p. 68).
They note that it was written not many years after the Reformation began, when not everything could suddenly be seen through and explained, and so on.

source_text: Nam aliud est, August. Confess. convitiis proscindere, vel quoquô modô debitam illius Auctoritatem elevare (quod à Reformatorum nemine unquam designatum est) aliud, non permittere velle, quòd humanum Scriptum, eóque errori obnoxium, cum infallibili Dei verbo, in eundem censum veniat. Rem omnem ex professo excutit Crocius Comment. cap. 36. a p. 497. Calvini Judicium de Augustana Confessione, ab eo promptè aliàs subscribenda, imò actu ipso subscripta (uti testatur in Epistola sua ad Martinum Schalingium Pastorem Ratisbonensem Anno 1557., Epistolarum Tomô, non ita pridem cum Operibus omnibus Amstelodami editô, p. m. 112.), quando Aug. Confessionem facem furiae Gallicae alicubi appellitat, genuino suo sensui restitutum lege, tùm apud Pareum Fren. p. 294, tùm apud Auctorem der ausführlichen Behauptung p. 74. & seqq. omniumq; plenissimè apud Joh. Crocium, Comment. saepius citat. p. 514. 515. 518.
english: For it is one thing to tear the Augsburg Confession with insults, or somehow to lower its due authority — which no Reformer ever set out to do — and another to refuse to let a human writing, liable to error, stand in the same rank as God's infallible word.
Crocius works the whole question through in Comm. cap. 36 from p. 497.

As for Calvin's judgment on the Augsburg Confession: he was ready to subscribe it at other times, and in fact did subscribe it (see his 1557 letter to Martin Schalingius, pastor at Regensburg, in the Letters volume lately edited at Amsterdam with the Opera, p. 112).

When elsewhere he calls the Augsburg Confession a torch of Gallic fury, read that restored to its genuine sense — in Pareus (Fren. p. 294), in the Ausführliche Behauptung (p. 74ff.), and most fully in Crocius (Comm. pp. 514, 515, 518).

source_text:
§. XIV.
POSTREMUM Annotationis nostrae MEMBRUM dilucidandum restat: Quô Sensu nonnulli, prae caeteris, Augustanae Confessionis Theologi salutari cupiant, seque salutent ipsos? Hoc ut tribus, quod aiunt, verbis expediamus, Characteristicis quibusdam Notis designatos eos dabimus praebebimusque conspiciendos. Sunt itaque
english: §. XIV. One last member of this Annotation still needs clearing: in what sense do some men — more than others — want to be greeted as Augsburg Confession theologians, and greet themselves that way?
To put it in three words, as the saying goes, we will mark them by a few characteristic notes and set them out to be seen.
They are, then, as follows.

source_text: [1.] QUI CUM LUTHERO, partim per Carolostadium, multa Wittenbergae, non tamen omnino privatâ, innovantem Auctoritate, partim per Zwinglium, in Articulorum suorum Explanatione Articuli XVII. paulò invidiosius (ut videri poterat) atque jactantius scribentem: Capi Ego Evangelium praedicare Anno Salutis XVI. supra M.D., scilicet tempore, cùm Lutheri nomen in nostris Regionibus ne auditum quidem erat; partim denique per Tigurinos, Bibliorum Sacrorum translationem, à se, Leone Juda Antesignano, adornatam, per Forschoverum Typographum, Luthero transmittentes, postquam hic suam cumprimis Bibliorum Versionem in publicum editam, ubique recipi cuperet; (de quibus singulis Calixtus in Judicio de Controv. Theolog. nó. 48. 53. 72.) irritato, & cum isti Sacramentum Eucharistiae, multis ac tetris abusibus, & superstitionibus hactenus apud Pontificios deformatum, restituere pristino nitori intenti, praesentiam Corporis & Sangvinis Christi negasse in eo viderentur, totô fervente & undiquaque adversarios premere annisô (sunt verba Calixti num. 47.) praesentiam Corporis Christi ita in Coena urgendam arbitrantur, ut novam & incommodam de Ubiquitate Sententiam, in aestu certaminum Luthero excisam, importunius urgeant; Nec verò cum Luthero mitiori & ex Buceri Declarationibus ac Confessione Tigurina facto certiori, praesentiam Corporis Christi in S. Coena nullam, quam localem naturalemque negatam esse, Sacramentali pariter ac Spirituali admissâ, ita sentientes, omnino ferendos esse arbitrantur, tanquam innocentes & puros, à Christo facilè liberandos, seque ab his quoque tolerari optant, in suam licèt Sententiam descendere nesciis. Vid. Hist. August. Conf. à Kirchn. Selneccer. & Chemnitio confectam & Calixto allegatam l. c. num. 62. in fine, collat. cum num. 63. 64. 65. 69. 71. 75.
english: [1.] Those who side with Luther against Carolstadt (innovating much at Wittenberg under authority that was not wholly private), against Zwingli (writing a little too spitefully and boastfully on Article XVII of his Articles' Explanation — "I began preaching the Gospel in A.D. 1516, when Luther's name had not even been heard in our regions"), and against the Zurichers (who sent Luther a Bible translation prepared under Leo Juda's lead and printed by Forschover, after Luther wanted his own published version received everywhere). On each of these see Calixtus, Judgment on Theological Controversies, nos. 48, 53, 72.

When those opponents, aiming to restore the Eucharist from papal abuses and superstitions to its old brightness, seemed to deny Christ's body and blood present in it, these men — "with all their heat, pressing adversaries on every side" (Calixtus, num. 47) — decide the bodily presence in the Supper must be pressed so hard that they push, too roughly, the new and awkward ubiquity opinion cut out for Luther in the heat of battle.

Nor will they bear at all those who follow the milder Luther, made surer by Bucer's Declarations and the Zurich Confession: that only a local, natural presence was denied in the Holy Supper, while sacramental and spiritual presence were both granted. Such people they will not treat as innocent and pure, easily freed by Christ; and they want tolerance from them too, though they themselves cannot come down into that milder view.
See the History of the Augsburg Confession by Kirchner, Selnecker, and Chemnitz, cited by Calixtus at num. 62 (end), with nums. 63–65, 69, 71, 75.

source_text: (2.) Qui cum PHILIPPO MELANCHTONE malè informato, & in Epistola ad Oecolampadium, Anno 1522. exarata, itemque in Epilogo Sententiarum collectarum ex Patribus, Anno 1530. de Sententia Buceri & Helvetiorum duriter pronunciante, proprietati verborum Coenae nimiùm inhaerent, ut nullam tropicam dictionem iis subesse autument, à se ipsis tamen nullâ ratione evitandam; Nec cum eodem Philippo melius informato & δευτέρας φροντίδας passo, in Epistola ad Urbanum Regium Aô. 1535. inque Epistolis ad Vitum Theodorum, maximè ea, quam Anno 1543. scripsit, & alibi passim necnon in Epistola ad Johannem Cratonem, anno mortem ejus praecedente 1559. τὸ ῥητὸν verborum Coenae Sacramentaliter accipiendum contendunt, & vetustatem longè hac de re aliter locutam fatentur, quàm recentiorem aetatem, quin Nazianzenum simpliciter ἀντίτυπα σώματος Χριστοῦ nominasse meminerunt, vid. Pezelium Argument. & Respons. Theolog. Parte VIII, a pag. 175. ad 190. & Epistolam Melanchtonis ad Cratonem scriptam in Epistolis & Judiciis Melanchtonis parte 2. p. 384. & 385. a Pezelio editis.
english: (2.) Those who cling with the badly informed Philip Melanchthon — harsh on Bucer's and the Swiss view in the 1522 letter to Oecolampadius and in the 1530 Epilogue of Sentences from the Fathers — so tightly to the bare property of the Supper words that they deny any tropical speech in them, even though they themselves cannot avoid figurative speech on other grounds.

And they will not follow the same Philip after better information and second thoughts (δευτέρας φροντίδας): in the 1535 letter to Urbanus Rhegius, in letters to Veit Dietrich (especially 1543), elsewhere, and in the 1559 letter to Johannes Crato the year before Melanchthon's death — where he holds that the letter (τὸ ῥητόν) of the Supper words is to be taken sacramentally, admits that the ancients spoke far otherwise than recent ages, and even recalls that Nazianzen simply called them ἀντίτυπα of Christ's body.
See Pezel, Arguments & Theological Responses VIII, pp. 175–190, and Melanchthon's letter to Crato in Letters & Judgments II, pp. 384–385 (Pezel).

source_text: (3.) Qui cum JOHANNE BRENTIO infaustum Ubiquitatis Corporis Christi, à Jacobo Fabro Stapulensi primò omnium excogitatum Dogma, teste Calixto, libellô citatô num. 38. & a Luthero, altero à Stapulensi, assertum, num. 40. postea tamen ab eodem missum factum, monente, praesentiam Corporis Christi in S. Coena non in disputatione de Ubiquitate, sed in veritate institutionis collocandam esse num. 44. eóque sopitum & diuturno silentio sepultum, è cineribus quasi suscitant, vel à Brentio & Jacobo Andreae resuscitatam de Ubiquitate, ut loquitur Calixtus num. 45. contentionem inflammant, inque ea proram & puppim Christianae Veritatis, ac sigillatim manducationis suae Oralis, reponunt; Nec tamen cum eodem, in Syngrammate Svevorum & in Exegesi in Johannem docent: Corpus Domini Fide comedi & Fidei praesens esse; Nam quaerit Brentius ad verba haec Johannis: (Caro mea verè est Cibus, & Sangvis meus verè est potus): Cujus? Respondet: Fidei: Nam fides edit Carnem Christi & bibit Sanguinem ejus, dum credit &c. Calixtus num. 53. in medio, subnectens proinde num. 56. ab initio: Haec profectò talia sunt, ut vix aliter verbis Sententiam suam explicatam eant Calviniani; Ore Corpus Christi manducari cavet Brentius dicere, adferre refugit, saltem fidei offerri & à fide docet accipi, & proptereà fidei praesens esse. Quod ipsum etiam contendunt Calviniani, hôc unô fortè discrimine, quòd fidem in Coelum Corpus Domini praesens intueri & complecti statuunt; Brentius autem fidei hîc in terris praesens esse & exhiberi docet.
english: (3.) Those who, with Johann Brenz, stir from the ashes the unhappy dogma of Christ's bodily ubiquity — first invented by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (Calixtus, booklet num. 38), asserted by Luther as second after Stapulensis (num. 40), then dropped by Luther with the warning that presence in the Holy Supper rests not on the ubiquity debate but on the truth of the institution (num. 44), and so put to sleep under long silence — or who inflame the ubiquity quarrel revived by Brenz and Jakob Andreae (Calixtus num. 45) and set in it the prow and stern of Christian truth, above all of their oral eating.

Yet they will not teach with the same Brenz in the Swabian Syngramma and the Exegesis on John: the Lord's body is eaten by faith and is present to faith. At John's words ("My flesh is truly food, and my blood truly drink") Brenz asks, "Whose?" and answers, "Faith's: for faith eats Christ's flesh and drinks his blood while it believes," etc. (Calixtus num. 53 mid).

Calixtus then adds (num. 56 open): these lines are such that Calvinists would scarcely explain their view in other words. Brenz is careful not to say Christ's body is chewed with the mouth; he refuses that claim; he teaches at least that it is offered to faith, received by faith, and therefore present to faith.

Calvinists press the same point, with perhaps this one difference: they hold that faith looks to and embraces the Lord's body present in heaven; Brenz teaches it is present and shown to faith here on earth.

source_text: (4.) Qui cum inquieto & ab ipso AUGUSTO, SAXONIAE ELECTORE, rixoso appellato (vid. Formul. Concord. Germanicam, anno proximè superiori editam Append. p. 119. in fine) FLACIO ILLYRICO, & acerbißimo, tantumque non delirante Philippo-Mastige: (de quo quam plurimi conquesti sunt Theologi, Wittenbergenses in Actis Colloquii Altenburgici passim, vid. Auctor der Aufführlicher Behauptung/ à pag. 64. ad 70. & cum Wittenbergensibus unà Lipsenses, Tractat. Germanico integro, Endlicher Bericht dictô, & Wittenbergae, literis Hans Luffts 1570. exscripto, Ipseque Melanchton, de turbis interim à Flacio excitatis, placidè satis locutus, cùm in Epistola ad Johann. Mathesium, inter Consilia & Judicia Melanchtonis exstante, Part. 2. pag. 257. tùm in Epistola, ejusdem manu exarata ad Ulricum Mordisium, &, ceu nondum edita, ex Bibliotheca Adami Christophori Jacobi, à Dn. Christiano Jünckero, in vita Lutheri p. 126. exhibita novissimè, hisce inter alia verbis: Libenter & ab ipsis Papistarum fucosis actionibus & Sycophantia Flaciana, discedam, inquit, quandocunque me Deus discedere volet, vel morientem, vel exulantem. Moriens, accedam ad Scholam Filii Dei & Coelestes Ecclesias; exulans inveniam, juvante Deo, hospitium apud meliores Flacio, qui minatur se effecturum, ut totâ Germania expellar: Oro Deum, ut vos regat atque tegat. Bene valete die 4. Novemb. 1558.) Variatam à Philippo Confessionem Augustanam, ob mutatum praecipuè Articulum Xmum, ex odio in Reformatos ἀσπόνδῳ, angue pejus ac cane refugiunt; Nec tamen meminisse volunt, hanc tàm cùm invariata, quà rem, eandem esse, judicibus Statibus Naumburgicis suprâ citatis, nec diffitente Mentzero Prolegom. in Exeges. A.C. p. m. 21. in med. quam nihil quicquam subsidii majoris ex ista, atq; ex hac, sententiae suae Reformatos vel petere, vel petere posse, vel petere velle; Nec decere Christianos Theologos propter ejusmodi Sycophantias, tunicam Christi inconsutilem, i. e. Ecclesiam Christi dilectam, dilectionisq; Christianae, jussu Christi, tenacissimam, in partes distrahere atque dilacerare.
english: (4.) Those who side with restless Flacius Illyricus — called quarrelsome even by Elector Augustus of Saxony himself (German Formula of Concord, appendix p. 119 end, edition of the year just past) — and with that bitter, almost raving scourge of Philip. Many theologians complained of him: the Wittenbergers throughout the Altenburg Colloquy acts; the Ausführlicher Behauptung author, pp. 64–70; the Leipzigers with them in the whole German Endlicher Bericht (Wittenberg, Hans Lufft, 1570); and Melanchthon himself, speaking calmly enough of Flacius's storms — in the letter to Johann Mathesius (Counsels & Judgments II, p. 257) and in a hand-written letter to Ulrich Mordisius, lately printed as unpublished from Adam Christoph Jacobi's library by Christian Jüncker in the Life of Luther, p. 126 — including: "Gladly will I leave both the painted deeds of the Papists and Flacian sycophancy whenever God wills me to go, dying or in exile. Dying, I go to the Son of God's school and the heavenly churches; in exile, God helping, I will find lodging with better men than Flacius, who threatens to drive me from all Germany. I pray God to rule and cover you. Farewell, 4 November 1558."
From implacable (ἀσπόνδῳ) hatred of the Reformed — worse than snake or dog — they flee Philip's Variata Augsburg Confession, mainly because Article X was changed.

Yet they will not remember that, as to substance, it is the same as the Invariata: so judged the Naumburg estates already cited, and Mentzer does not deny it (Prolegomena to the Exegesis of the A.C., p. 21 mid) — that the Reformed neither seek nor can seek nor wish to seek any greater support for their view from one edition than from the other.
Nor does it become Christian theologians, for such sycophancies, to rip and tear Christ's seamless tunic — that is, his beloved church, most tenacious of Christian love by his command — into pieces.

source_text: (5.) Qui cum PATRIBUS BERGENSIBUS Formulam Concordiae, verum istud ἔριδος omnisque contentionis Protestanticæ pomum infaustissimum, quippe de Manducatione & Omnipraesentia Corporis Christi Corporalibus famosum dogmatibus, ipsâ Augustana Confessione, horum Dogmatum penitus ignara vacuâq;, antiquiorem ducunt; nec quicquam morantur, tàm olim, quàm nunc, etiam à suis, cùm Ecclesiis, harumque Doctoribus piissimis atque doctissimis, tum Principibus & Imperii Romano-Germanici Statibus, maximo cùm zelo contradictum esse, hodieque à nonnullis contradici, (vid. Joh. Crocium in Tractatu Germanico à pag. 99. & in Comment. August. Confess. passim, praecipuè pag. 282.) ipsam etiam Formulam Concordiae, tam mutatum August. Confessionis Articulum X., i. e. Germanico Idiomati Prototypi haud respondentem, (propter quem tamen Articulum mutatum, adeò acerbè in Variatam Confessionem Formulistae invehuntur) retinuisse, quam ipsam per se creberrimas mutationes ac variationes passam esse. Vid. Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung à pag. 26. ad 36.
english: (5.) Those who with the Bergen Fathers rank the Formula of Concord — that most unhappy apple of strife (ἔριδος) and of all Protestant quarrel, notorious for bodily manducation and omnipresence of Christ's body — older than the Augsburg Confession itself, which knows nothing of those dogmas and is empty of them.

They care nothing that their own side has contradicted it with great zeal both formerly and now — churches and their most pious, learned doctors, and also princes and estates of the Romano-German Empire — and that some still contradict it today (Crocius, German tract from p. 99; Commentary on the Augsburg Confession passim, esp. p. 282).

Nor do they care that the Formula itself kept the changed Article X of the Augsburg Confession — which does not match the German of the prototype — the very change for which Formulists attack the Variata so bitterly — and that the Formula itself has suffered very frequent mutations and variations.
See the Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung, pp. 26–36.

source_text: (6.) Qui denique per HAEC UNIVERSA & se solos Orthodoxos esse, & sua Commenta omnia ad Fundamentum Fidei, sive Antecedenter, sive Concomitanter, sive Consequenter, pertinere sibi imaginati, quotquot Formulae Concordiae, rectius Discordiae appellandae, non assurgunt, utut caetera Aug. Confess. Invariatam perinde atque Variatam sincerissimo animo profitantur, à se arcent ac damnant, Schismate, ut carnaliori multò, ita & infeliciori, à Syncretistis ferè juxtà ac Reformatis, quàm Pontificii à Protestantibus, semet separantes; Ab his ipsis tamen, à quibus semet sejungunt, studiosissimè pariter atque indefessè, non tantum ad mutuam Tolerantiam, sed & Complexum Fraternum & Unionem Ecclesiasticam, utcunque inviti, per & propter Deum Christumq; ejus, (demonstratô Sociorum August. Confess. omnium Consensu Fundamentali) invitati invitandique; Quo de in sequentibus proximè Annotationibus plura.
english: (6.) Finally, those who by THESE UNIVERSALS imagine that they alone are orthodox, and that all their commentaries belong to the foundation of the faith — whether before it, with it, or after it — and who shut out and damn everyone who will not rise to the Formula of Concord (better called Discord), even when those others sincerely confess both the Invariata and the Variata Augsburg Confession in everything else.
They cut themselves off by a schism more carnal and more unhappy from syncretists and from the Reformed almost alike — worse than the cut Papists make from Protestants.

Yet from the very people they leave they are invited, and ought to be invited, as steadily as without tiring — however unwilling — not only to mutual tolerance but to a brotherly embrace and church union, through and for the sake of God and his Christ (once the fundamental consent of all Augsburg Confession associates is shown).
On that, more in the Annotations that follow next.

source_text: Annotationis praecedentis, utpotè paulò prolixioris breve Compendium, jampridem, Decem Thesibus, in Vernacula nostra, ab Excellentissimo quondam hujus Universitatis Doctore & Professore Theologo, B. Gregorio Gregorii Franco, comprehensum, ac Tractatui cuidam suo Polemico, publicis typis exscripto, Subjunctum.
english: Here is a short compendium of the preceding Annotation — which ran a little long — cast long ago into Ten Theses in our vernacular by the late excellent doctor and theology professor of this University, B. Gregorius Gregorii Francus, and printed as an appendix to one of his polemical tracts.

source_text:
I.
Quanquam Augustanae Confessionis exemplar, An. 1530. primùm exhibitum, ad ann. usque 1540, in quibusdam sensim auctum emendatumque fuerit, ex eo tamen tempore in posteriori correcto exemplari, per centum annos, ne litera quidem immutata est.
english: I. Though the Augsburg Confession text first shown in 1530 was, in places, gradually enlarged and corrected through 1540, from that time the later corrected exemplar has not changed so much as a letter for a hundred years.

source_text:
II.
Duo interim Exemplaria propriè loquendô ab Electoribus, Principibus & Statibus Imperii agnita & exhibita sunt, inque scriptis Lutheri & Melanchthonis & Actis Imperii reperiunda: Prius Wittenbergae An. 31. impressum; Posterius An. 40. & 41. auctum Caesarique Ferdinando I. unà cum priori, An. 1561. Naumburgô transmissum, cui ad hanc usq; diem nihil additum ademptumque fuit.
english: II. Properly speaking, two exemplars have been acknowledged and presented by the Electors, Princes, and Imperial Estates, and they stand in Luther's and Melanchthon's writings and in the Imperial Acts.

The earlier was printed at Wittenberg in 1531; the later, enlarged in 1540 and 1541, was sent with the earlier one to Emperor Ferdinand I at Naumburg in 1561 — and to this day nothing has been added to it or taken from it.

source_text:
III.
Duo illa exemplaria, non duplicem, sed unam eandemq; Confessionem continent, nec posterius à priori, substantialibus fidei articulis, sed solis verbis clariorique explicatione, differt.
IV.
Exemplar Augustanae Confessionis, Formulae Concordiae insertum, in quibusdam quidem verbis, ab eo, quod Wittebergae An. 31. impressum in Tomis Lutheri invenitur, est diversum; in substantialibus tamen plenè cum eodem convenit.
english: III. Those two exemplars are not two confessions, but one and the same: the later differs from the earlier not in the substance of the faith's articles, but only in wording and clearer explanation.
IV. The Augsburg Confession text slotted into the Formula of Concord does differ in some words from the 1531 Wittenberg printing in Luther's volumes; in substance, though, it fully matches that text.

source_text:
V.
Qui alterutram harum Confessionum recipit, Socius est Augustanae Confessionis, nec religiosa Imperii pace jure excludi potest.
VI.
Electores, Principes, ac Status Imperii, adauctam Confessionem aequè ac priorem, publice professi sunt.
english: V. Anyone who receives either of these Confessions is an associate of the Augsburg Confession, and cannot lawfully be shut out of the Empire's Religious Peace.
VI. Electors, Princes, and Imperial Estates have publicly professed the enlarged Confession no less than the earlier one.

source_text:
VII.
Nec Recessus, nec Acta Edictave Imperii, vel variatae, vel invariatae Augustanae Confessionis (Sub bisputa Denominationibus) mentionem ullam faciunt.
VIII.
Recens quorundam Evangelicorum, Bergensi Formulae addictorum doctrina, de orali manducatione, & ubiquitate Corporis Christi, nec in priori, nec auctiori Confessione, multò minùs in ejusdem Repetitione & Corpore Doctrinae Philippi reperitur; Unde nec Reformati Augustanae Confessionis Socii, ob haec duo dogmata negata, pace Imperii excludi possunt.
english: VII. Neither Imperial Recesses nor Acts or Edicts ever mention a Variata or Invariata Augsburg Confession under those contested labels.

VIII. The recent teaching of certain Evangelicals bound to the Bergen Formula — oral eating and the ubiquity of Christ's body — is in neither the earlier nor the enlarged Confession, and still less in the Repetitio or in Philip's Corpus Doctrinae.
So the Reformed, as associates of the Augsburg Confession, cannot be shut out of the Imperial Peace for denying those two dogmas.

source_text:
IX.
Utut Ubiquitismus, & quicquid ei annexum est, ingens error sit, quoniam tamen per actum quendam solennem, in Generali quadam aut Nationali Synodo, nondum improbatus est, propugnatores quoque ejus adeò diversimodè de eo loquuntur, ut quid propriè statuant, intelligi vix queat, aestimandum est, tolerari adhuc, & approbantes istum, nihilo secius Augustanae Confessionis Sociis annumerandos esse.
X.
Quemadmodum & D. Lutherus, & M. Phil. Melanchthon, Augustanae Confessionis Socii fuêre, tales ab omnibus habiti, eique ad finem usque viae ex intimo corde addicti permansêre, licèt de modo exhibitionis Corporis Christi in S. Coena, dissenserint; Ita Reformati aequè ac Lutherani Socii Augustanae Confessionis permanent, quamvis in eodem, & aliis quibusdam quaestionibus scholasticis, non penitus inter se conveniant.
Addendum & emendandum:
Pag. 13. lin. 5. Pro: Christianum Pontanum, lege: Christianum Bajerum, postquam SERENISSIMUS ELECTOR ab IMPERATORE CAROLO V. precibus impetrasset, ut Augustana Confessio, in Germania inq Augusta Vindelicorum Civitate, etiam Germanico Idiomate prelegeretur. Vid. Clar. Pipping/ in der Einleitung zu den Symbol. Schrifften Lutherischer Kirchen.
english: IX. Ubiquitism and whatever hangs on it may be a huge error; still, no solemn act of a general or national synod has yet condemned it, and its defenders talk about it in such different ways that one can hardly tell what they actually hold.
So it should still be tolerated, and those who approve it should nonetheless be counted among the associates of the Augsburg Confession.

X. Luther and Melanchthon were associates of the Augsburg Confession, held as such by everyone, and stayed heart-devoted to it to the end of their course, even though they disagreed on how Christ's body is exhibited in the Holy Supper.
In the same way the Reformed, no less than the Lutherans, remain associates of the Augsburg Confession, even when they do not fully agree on that point and on certain other school questions.

Addendum and correction: p. 13, line 5 — for Christianum Pontanum read Christianum Bajerum, after the Most Serene Elector obtained by petition from Emperor Charles V that the Augsburg Confession should also be read aloud in German in Germany and in the city of Augsburg. See Clar. Pipping, Einleitung zu den Symbol. Schrifften Lutherischer Kirchen.

source_text:
ANNOTATIO II.
De Sociorum Confessionis Augustanae Consensu Fundamentali & Dissensu Praeter-fundamentali, hujusque Ortu, Progressu & Exitu,
Ad Pag. Autoris 332. & 333.
§. I.
Consensus Fundamentalis Sociorum Confessionis Augustanae, respicit Fundamentum Christianae Religionis, seu Doctrinae Christianae, tam Theoreticae, quàm Practicae, quippe quarum Doctrinarum aliae Fundamentales, aliae Fundamentatae sunt. PRIORES, seu Fundamentales, accipiuntur VEL SENSU SCRIPTURARIO, & sunt Doctrinae de Christo, unico Salvatore nostro, Deo & Homine, reliquis Fundamentum praebiturae omnium summum, seu primum, 1. Cor. 3. v. 11. Aliud equidem Fundamentum nemo potest ponere &c. Nam per Christum hoc in loco, non solam Personam Christi, sed potissimum Doctrinam de Christo intelligendam esse, patet, tum ex Antecedentibus, tum ex Consequentibus. Ex Antecedentibus quidem: Quandoquidem Fundamentum (Christus) à Paulo, ceu prudenti Architecto, positum dicitur; Erat autem à Paulo non Christus ipse positus, sed Doctrina seu Evangelium de Christo, ceu Fundamentum omnium Doctrinarum Christianae Religionis, Doctrinae de Christo superaedificandarum. Ex Consequentibus, quia alii aliique, dicuntur Fundamento superaedificaturi, Aurum, Argentum, Lignum, Stipulas, i. e. Fundamentali de Christo Doctrinae, Fundamentatas plurimas, alias preciosiores ac utiles, alias minus preciosas ac futiles. Quin idem probatur ex Eph. 2. ubi unô eôdemque vigesimo versiculo, tàm Apostoli & Prophetae, i. e. Doctrinae Apostolorum & Prophetarum praecipuae, non autem Personae eorum, Fundamentum salutantur, quam Christus Lapis Angularis, i. e. Doctrina de Christo Principalissima & maximè Fundamentalis dicitur.
english: ANNOTATION II. On the Augsburg Confession associates' fundamental consensus and their praeter-fundamental dissent — and on that dissent's origin, progress, and outcome. To the Author's pp. 332–333.

§. I. The associates' fundamental consensus looks to the foundation of the Christian religion — Christian doctrine, theoretical and practical — of which some doctrines are fundamentals and others are built on them (fundamentata).

The former, taken in the scriptural sense, are the doctrines concerning Christ, our only Saviour, God and Man: the highest, first foundation for everything else ([[1 Cor. 3:11 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 3:11]]: "For other foundation can no man lay," &c.).

Here "Christ" means chiefly the doctrine about Christ, not only his person — clear from what precedes and what follows. Paul as wise architect is said to have laid the foundation (Christ); what he laid was not Christ himself but the gospel-doctrine about Christ, the base on which other Christian doctrines are built.

What follows confirms it: others are to build on that foundation gold, silver, wood, stubble — many things founded on the fundamental doctrine of Christ, some precious and useful, some cheaper and futile.

[[Eph. 2:20 >> Bible:Ephesians 2:20]] says the same in one verse: Apostles and Prophets (i.e. their chief doctrines, not their persons) are called foundation, and Christ the cornerstone — that is, the doctrine of Christ is named the principal and most fundamental.

source_text: VEL SENSU THEOLOGICO, & sunt Doctrinae, tam ad Religionem vel Fidem Christianam constituendam, quàm ad Fidei Christianae Finem, Animarum nostrarum Salutem consequendam, omninò necessariae, indeque communiter dicendae, modò Fundamentales Fidei, respectu ad Objectum, Fundamentato intrinsecum & essentiale; modò Fundamentales Salutis, respectu ad Finem, Fundamentato partim intrinsecum & essentialem, partim extrinsecum & extraessentialem, habito. Necessitatem autem istarum omnem determinante, in Scriptura S., Deô solô, idque vel explicitè, vel implicitè, per obviam cuivis consequentiam; itemque exclusivo non minus Sensu, quàm positivo, ut & dicat Deus, quaenam Necessariae Doctrinae sint; & non dictas ab eo Necessarias, sive explicitè, sive implicitè, eô ipsô à Necessitate Fidei & Salutis, non tamen pariter à varii Gradûs Utilitate, exemptas velit. Neque enim vel probabile est, vel ullo modo admittendum, ut Deus, universae Scripturae S. unicus quidem Autor habitus, in qua & Necessaria ad Fidem Salutemque, & minus necessaria promiscuè traduntur, necessaria etiam nonnulla subindè apertè significantur, vel non omnia necessaria ullo modo definivisse, sicque necessaria à minus necessariis non satis distinxisse, vel definitionem distinctionemque hanc humano arbitrio permisissse credendus sit; praesertim cùm cuncta, ad salutem necessaria, promiscuè, eóque ut talia, tradiderit. Vide haec fusius edocta Inquisit. in Arminian. Annot. XVII.
english: Or take fundamentals in the theological sense: doctrines wholly necessary both to constitute Christian religion or faith and to reach faith's end — the salvation of our souls.

Hence they are commonly called either fundamentals of faith (toward the object: the intrinsic, essential thing founded) or fundamentals of salvation (toward the end: the thing founded partly intrinsic/essential, partly extrinsic/extra-essential).

God alone in Holy Scripture fixes all that necessity — explicitly or implicitly, by a consequence open to anyone — and in an exclusive sense no less than a positive one: so God both names which doctrines are necessary and, by not naming others as necessary (explicitly or implicitly), exempts them from faith-and-salvation necessity, though not from usefulness of every degree.

It is neither likely nor admissible that God, sole author of all Scripture — where necessities for faith and salvation are mixed with lesser matters, and some necessities are at times marked openly — either failed to define all necessities at all (and so failed to distinguish them from the less necessary) or left that definition and distinction to human whim; especially since he handed down everything needed for salvation promiscuously, and as such. See this taught more fully in the Inquisition into the Arminians, Annotation XVII.

source_text:
§. II.
Hinc illi demùm Fundamentaliter in Religione Fideque Christiana consentire Sensu Theologicô dicuntur, qui in omnibus à Deo ad Fidem & Salutem dictis necessariis consentiunt; Necessaria autem nec alia, nec plura, nec pauciora arbitrantur, quàm quae DEus talia in verbo suo jussit esse. E contrario, isti Fundamentaliter dissentiunt, qui vel in Necessariis Fidei & Salutis, à DEO sic dictis, discrepant, negando vel omnia, vel quaedam eorum, idque, vel quà Veritatem, vel quà Necessitatem; vel praeter Necessaria Divina, alia, citra verbum DEi, ceu talia, cudunt obtruduntque. Horum Dissensuum prior Juris magis est; posterior magis Facti. Priori modô Fundamentaliter dissentiunt à Protestantibus Sociniani; Posteriori ab iisdem Pontificii: Protestantes verò, seu Evangelici, Fundamentaliter inter se convenire intelliguntur utrôque modô, excipiendis tamen Protestantibus iis, qui Dogmata quaedam, sibi domestica, neque in Scriptura Sacra, vel quoad Veritatem, nedum Necessitatem, fundata, Necessaria nihilominus urgent, & talia abnuentes à se separant damnantque, eô ipsô, Fundamento, si non Fidei, strictè sic dictae, seu Theoriae Christianae, Charitatis tamen, seu Praxeos (quae Religioni Christianae, adeoque Fidei Christianae latius dictae, pars altera est) excidentes.
english: §. II. Those finally are said to agree fundamentally in Christian religion and faith, in the theological sense, who agree in everything God has called necessary to faith and salvation — and who count as necessary neither other things, nor more, nor fewer, than God has commanded to be such in his word.

Those dissent fundamentally who either diverge from the necessaries of faith and salvation so named by God, denying all or some of them as to truth or as to necessity; or who, beyond the divine necessaries, forge and push other things as necessary apart from God's word.
Of these dissents the former is more a matter of right; the latter more of fact. Socinians dissent fundamentally from Protestants in the former way; Romanists in the latter.

Protestants, or Evangelicals, are understood to agree fundamentally among themselves in both ways — except those who still press as necessary certain house-dogmas of their own, founded neither in Scripture as to truth nor (still less) as to necessity, and who cut off and damn those who refuse them: thereby falling from the foundation, if not of faith strictly so called (Christian theory), then of charity or practice (the other part of the Christian religion, and of Christian faith in the wider sense).

source_text:
§. III.
Ita Protestantes inter se Fundamentaliter convenire à priori ostensum est; Constare idem à posteriori potest inductione Capitum Doctrinae Christianae Necessariorum Generalium: Enimverò conveniunt inter se (1.) Principio cognoscendi Christiana Dogmata omnia, saltèm necessaria cuncta, primo & unicô adaequato, nempe Scripturâ S. ideò unanimibus votis, tam sufficienti atque perfectâ, quàm satis perspicua Regulâ & normâ credendorum pariter ac agendorum Christianorum omnium necessariorum, Protestantibus habita; Secus ac Christianis reliquis quibuscunque, vel Synonymicè, vel aequivocè sic dictis, à Protestantibus in eo dissidentibus, quod vel principio Scripturae aliud coordinant, Scilicet Traditiones seu Verbum non-Scriptum, vel hoc alteri subordinant, puta vel Lumini Nativo, i. e. Rationi, vel Lumini Fictitio, i. e.
