source_text: Quandoquidem ab ipso Spiritu S. dissidiorum non minus ac calumniarum, quam homicidiorum ex istis pullulantium, Pater, Diabolus nuncupatur Joh. 8. 44. non hominibus duntaxat inhians, Leonis rugientis ad instar 1. Pet. 5. adque opera sua incitans, Jacob. 4. quin permittente ex justo judicio Deô, operationem etiam suam in filiis infidelitatis perque eos peragens, Eph. 2, 2. collat. cum 5, 6. inque Judam etiam aliquem, Proditorem Christi, illapsus, Joh. 13; sed rixas insuper in specie excitans, alens, promovensque; ob id, respectu primae earum scaturiginis, denominandas Diabolicas. Jac. 3, 15. hincque tritico Veritatis ac Pacis, Mendaciorum ac Dissidiorum Zizania interferens.
english: For the Holy Spirit Himself names the Devil father of dissensions no less than of slanders and of the murders that sprout from them (John 8:44).

He does not only gape after people like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5) and spur them to his works (James 4); God permitting by just judgment, he also works in the sons of unbelief and through them (Ephesians 2:2 with 5:6), and even entered a Judas, betrayer of Christ (John 13).

Moreover he stirs up, feeds, and pushes quarrels of that kind — so, from their first spring, they are rightly called diabolical (James 3:15) — sowing tares of lies and dissension in the wheat of truth and peace.

source_text: Ut Proinde quaesituro: Quis molimina Pacis supra recensita demolitus sit, haud ineptè verbis Christi respondeas: πονηρὸν Inimicumque communem id perpetrâsse, Matth. 13, 28.
english: So to anyone who asks who wrecked the peace attempts recounted above, you may aptly answer with Christ’s words:
the wicked one — our common enemy — did it (Matthew 13:28).
Stop before §. II (internal fountains: pravity of will and error of intellect).

source_text:
§. II.
Posteriores, Fontes dixeris alios, ex primis Actionum humanarum Principiis, Intellectui & Voluntati inhaerentibus vitiis communibus duobus, Pravitate & Errore exoriturus; alios Rivulos, ex fontibus memoratis scaturientes, eosque numero plures.
english: §. II. The later obstacles you may call other fountains — arising from two common vices in the first principles of human action, intellect and will: pravity and error.
From those fountains spring still more rivulets, greater in number.

source_text: Fontium binorum Priorem, Pravitatem Voluntatis facio-liberam, non minus sub Foedere Gratiae, quam Operum, errorem Intellectûs praevertentem: cum vel ipsius Foederis divini cujuscunque cum homine initi natura, tantum Luminis in intellectu humano supponat, quantum sufficit Pravitati voluntatis malitiosae vel cohibendae, vel repellendae, ut sic ad rixas sacras & dissidia Ecclesiastica praeter necessitatem, etiamsi instigante Diabolo, progressus, sciat, se non invitum, vel per errorem intellectûs, vel per Diaboli persuasionem, sed per liberam potius electionem suam ac προαίρεσιν, ad eandem provolâsse, promoventibus dissidiorum negotium rivulis majoribus tribus ex pravitate Voluntatis emanantibus & Johanni Apostolo probè notatis, hôc locô, inverso ordine recensendis:
english: Of the two fountains, the first is the free-acting pravity of the will — which, under the covenant of grace no less than of works, runs ahead of intellect’s error.
For any divine covenant with man presupposes enough light in the mind to restrain or repel malicious will-pravity.

So whoever has gone on to needless sacred quarrels and church splits — even with the Devil prodding — should know he rushed in not unwillingly, nor merely by intellect’s mistake or the Devil’s talk, but by his own free choice and προαίρεσις.
Three larger rivulets from will-pravity, well marked by the Apostle John, promote that work of dissension; we list them here in reverse order:

source_text:
Scilicet (1.) Fastu vitae, seu ambitione, sacro etiam ordini ut plurimùm adhaerente (uti constat in Pharisaeis Matth. 23, 5, 6, 7.) Veritati ac Paci perquam infesto Joh. 5, 44. & 7, 18. rixarum verò feracissimo 2. Tim. 3, 1, 2, 3. Ut vel ex vulgato isto, in Arrium rixatorem dicto, patet:
Quaeritur Haereticus (Schismaticus,) quare sit factus Arius,
In promptu Causa est, ambitiosus erat.
english: (1.) Pride of life — or ambition — which usually clings even to the sacred order (as in the Pharisees, Matt. 23:5–7).
It is most hostile to truth and peace (John 5:44; 7:18) and most fertile of quarrels (2 Tim. 3:1–3).
That common couplet on quarrelsome Arius makes the same point: ask why the heretic (schismatic) Arius became what he was — the ready answer is, he was ambitious.

source_text: (2.) Cupiditate oculorum, intellige Spiritualium, seu animae, verbô unô, Curiositate in Sacris nimiâ, ex ambitione ortâ, contra istud Apostoli ad Rom. 12, 3. μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ’ ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν (nam inflatus languet circa quaestiones. 1. Tim. 6, 3. 4. 5. Episcopo fugiendas, 2. Tim. 2, 23. 24. Tit. III. 9.), duo admodum mala, Paci Ecclesiasticae quam maximè infensa, progeneratura, dogmatum scil. Theologicorum multiplicationem eximiam; & noviter inventorum malesanam deperitionem.
english: (2.) Lust of the eyes — meaning spiritual lusts of the soul; in a word, excessive curiosity in sacred things, born of ambition — against Romans 12:3: do not think beyond what you ought, but think unto sobriety.
For the puffed-up man languishes among questions (1 Tim. 6:3–5) that a bishop must flee (2 Tim. 2:23–24; Titus 3:9).
This breeds two evils most hostile to church peace: an extraordinary multiplication of theological dogmas, and an unhealthy doting on novelties.

source_text: (3.) Cupiditate Carnis i. e. rerum Carnalium & mundanarum, unâ φιλαργυρίας vitiositate ab Apostolo redargutâ, quam Pharisaeis falsisque Doctoribus propriam Luc. 16. v. 14., & cum φιλαυτίᾳ cohaerentem. 2. Timoth. 3, 2, à Christianis Doctoribus alienam cupit Petrus 1. Pet. 5, 2.
english: (3.) Lust of the flesh — craving carnal and worldly goods — plus the love-of-money the Apostle rebukes as the mark of Pharisees and false teachers (Luke 16:14).
It sticks close to self-love (φιλαυτία, 2 Tim. 3:2), which Peter insists Christian teachers must keep far from (1 Pet. 5:2).

source_text: Posterior Fons, Error Intellectus est, quem pronus incurrit, quisquis voluntatis pravitati habenas laxat, sicuti vice versa, malitiam detestatus, veritati propior imminet. PS. 25. v. 14. Matt. 5. v. 8. Joh. 7. v. 17. Subnascitur autem error proximè ex praejudiciis, affectuum praedominio etiam educatione & informatione perversis, lectione librorum calumniosorum, hisque similibus;
english: The second fountain is error of intellect — which anyone who loosens the reins to will-pravity is apt to fall into; conversely, whoever hates malice draws nearer the truth (Ps. 25:14; Matt. 5:8; John 7:17).
Error is born nearby from prejudices, passions in the saddle, warped schooling and teaching, the reading of slanderous books, and the like.

source_text: Perficitur vel malè & aegrè apprehendendo res Theologicas, adque amussim rerum terrestrium dijudicando, cum Nicodemo Joh. 3, 12. & Capernaitis Joh. 6. vel perversè componendo & apparenter contradictoria, extra Scripturam, conciliando. e. g. effata Christi duo Matt. 26. v. 11. & 28. v. 20. confictione duplicis Corporis Christi, visibilis & invisibilis, concilianda a. quàm facillimè distinctione Biblica inter duplicem Christi naturam, tàm Paulo Rom. 1. v. 3. 4. & Cap. 9. 5. quàm Petro 1. C. 3. v. 18. & Cap. 4. 1. recepta. Vel Confundendo diversa nec satis distinguendo, e. g. inter Veritates Theologicas quascunque, & inter Fundamentales magisque necessarias; vel Colligendo ineptè, e. g. negari omnipotentiam Divinam, dum de Dei voluntate & Revelatione in Dogmatibus quibusdam ambigitur; item, dissentientem omnia pro veris certisque habere, quae vel rectè, vel malè, ex Sententia ejus colliguntur. &c.
english: It is finished either by grasping theological things badly and weakly and measuring them by earthly standards — with Nicodemus (John 3:12) and the Capernaites (John 6) —

or by twisting apparent contradictions into harmony outside Scripture: for example Christ’s two sayings in Matt. 26:11 and 28:20, reconciled by inventing a double body of Christ, visible and invisible, though the biblical distinction of Christ’s two natures (Paul, Rom. 1:3–4; 9:5; Peter, 1 Pet. 3:18; 4:1) does it far more easily.
Or by confusing what differs and not distinguishing enough — e.g. any theological truths whatever versus the fundamental and more necessary ones;

or by inferring clumsily — e.g. that God’s omnipotence is denied when his will and revelation in some dogmas are debated; or that a dissenter holds as sure everything rightly or wrongly drawn from his opinion; and so on.
Stop before §. III (further rivulets from either fountain, noted by our Author).

source_text:
§. III.
Ex utroque Obicum Fonte alii aliique Rivuli, consimilem aquam trahentes, deducuntur, Autori nostro notati.
english: §. III. From either fountain of these obstacles still other rivulets run down, drawing the same kind of water — ones our Author notes.

source_text: Ex Priori (1.) Errorem quemvis, in haeresin pro libidine vertere, vel dissensum minoris momenti, in fundamentalem; In fundamentalem, inquam, quando vel omnino fictus est dissensus eoque nullus, vel Verbalis tantùm, vel ad summum, Modum rei concernens.
english: From the first fountain: (1.) Stretch any error into heresy at will, or turn a lesser dissent into a fundamental one.
“Fundamental,” I mean, when the dissent is wholly feigned and so none at all, or only verbal, or at most about the mode of the thing.

source_text: (2.) Haeresi practica laborare, i. e. Charitatis judicio nullum locum relinquere, omniaque à dissentientibus dicta in pessinam quamque partem interpretari.
english: (2.) Labor under practical heresy — leave no room for charity’s judgment, and take everything dissenters say in the worst possible sense.

source_text: Ex posteriori [1.] Sensu suô abundare, novitates suas bonâ fide aliis instillare, in Ecclesiae Pacisque Ecclesiasticae praejudicium.
english: From the second fountain: [1.] Swell with your own sense, and in good faith drip your novelties into others — to the hurt of the church and of church peace.

source_text: (2.) Adiaphoris Ecclesiasticis, ob inolitam consuetudinem, pertinaciter, etiam ubi periculum peccandi est, itemque cum apertissima adversus Magistratum Superiorem inobedientia, per Zelum, ignorantiae debitum, inhaerere.
english: (2.) Cling stubbornly to church adiaphora from long habit, even where sin is a real risk,
and even with open disobedience to the higher magistrate, under a zeal that is really owed to ignorance.

source_text: Plura collige ex Ramo Olivae Septentrionalis Joh. Matthaei Stregensis Episcopi, Bacca quartâ, Sexta, Septima & Octava.
english: Gather more from the Northern Olive-branch of Johannes Matthiae, Bishop of Strängnäs — berries four, six, seven, and eight.
Stop before Annotatio V (Limites Consociationis Ecclesiasticae).

source_text:
ANNOTATIO V.
De Limitibus Consociationis Ecclesiasticae ad pag. 347.–352.
english: ANNOTATION V.
Concerning the bounds of church Consociation — Autor pages 347 through 352.

source_text:
§. I.
Limites, Obicibus oppositi, intelliguntur de Jure, uti Obices de facto. Quemadmodum limes injustus, obicis, ita obex justus, limitis naturam induit. Hinc limites Consociationis Ecclesiasticae hoc loco intelliguntur, non quales actu & de facto dantur, sed quales jure, & quidem Divinô ac Ecclesiastico, dari & possent, & debent.
english: §. I. Limits stand opposite Obstacles: limits are understood of right, obstacles of fact.
An unjust boundary acts like an obstacle; a just obstacle acts like a limit.
So here the limits of church consociation are not whatever happens to obtain in practice, but what by divine and church right can and ought to be set.

source_text: Ita verò intellecti, vel sumuntur Materialiter, pro rebus, seu Articulis Christ. Religionis, Consociationem Ecclesiasticam juste limitantibus, seu ad justos terminos redigentibus, intraque eosdem continentibus; vel Formaliter pro limitatione ipsâ, seu actu limitandi vario graduque.
english: Taken that way, limits are either Material — the things or articles of the Christian religion that justly bound church consociation and keep it inside those bounds —
or Formal — the limitation itself, the act of limiting in its various degrees.

source_text:
§. II.
Res Consociationem Ecclesiasticam limitantes, seu justos ei terminos figentes, non sunt Veritates Christianae quaecunque, sed Fundamentales, seu Fundamentalia Fidei Christianae dogmata, Annot. 2dâ descripta. Talia dari, ab aliis scilicet Fidei Christianae dogmatibus minùs fundamentalibus diversa, hisque contradistinguenda, probatum alibi, tùm ab Autore nostro Tract. de Fundamentalibus, Disp. 1. & 2. itemque Specim. Strict. contra Episcop. Condomiensem a. p. 63. ad 70. tùm à nobis, Dissert. de Pace Eccles. Cap. 7. & in Inquisit. in Arminianis. Annot. 17. omniumque Protestantium calculô confirmatum, etiam adversus Pontificios,
english: §. II. What sets just bounds for church consociation is not every Christian truth whatever, but the Fundamental dogmas of the Christian faith (described in Annotation 2).

That such fundamentals exist, distinct from less fundamental dogmas, has been shown elsewhere — by our Author’s Tract on Fundamentals (Disp. 1–2) and his Specimen against the Bishop of Condom (pp. 63–70), and by us in the Dissertation on Church Peace (ch. 7) and the Inquiry into the Arminians (Annot. 17) —
and all Protestants reckon the same way, even against the Roman party,

source_text: Fundamentales, sive auctoritate Divinâ eâque immediatâ, sive naturâ suâ talia, quòd fidem Christianam fundant, per se agnoscentes nulla, omnia verò Dogmata fidei Christianae maxima minimaque, tùm quà Veritatem, tùm quà Necessitatem, aut Fundamentalitatem, ab Auctoritate Ecclesiae Romanae suspendentes, quâ fit, ut quod vel fidem Christianam contingit minimum, vel fidei Christianae adversum est, illud nihilominus, hôc non obstante, per Constantiense quoddam, vel Papale Concilium, fidei Christianae essentiale evadat vel maximum,
english: who own no fundamentals in themselves — neither by immediate divine authority nor by their nature as founding the Christian faith —
but hang every dogma of the faith, great or small, as to truth, necessity, or fundamentality, on the authority of the Roman Church.
So what barely touches the Christian faith, or even runs against it, can still, through some Constance or papal council, become essential to that faith — even the greatest point.

source_text: eóque porrò illi, qui e. g. affirmat cum Paulo, in Eucharistiae Sacramento remanere substantiam Panis & Vini, 1. Cor. XI. 26. 27. 28. haut aliter, ac si fundamentum fidei Christianae integrum conculcâsset, anathema terribile per Concilium Tridentinum Session. XIII. Canon. II. annunciatum sit his verbis: Si quis dixerit, in Sacrosancto Eucharistiae Sacramento remanere Substantiam panis & vini unà cum Corpore & Sanguine Domini nostri Jesu Christi, negaveritque mirabilem illam & singularem Conversionem totius Substantiae panis in Corpus & totius substantiae vini in Sanguinem manentibus duntaxat Speciebus panis & vini: quam quidem Conversionem Catholica Ecclesia aptissimè Transsubstantiationem appellat, anathema sit. pag. m. 130.
english: Thus someone who affirms with Paul that in the Eucharist the substance of bread and wine remains (1 Cor. 11:26–28) is treated no milder than if he had trampled the whole foundation of the Christian faith:

Trent, Session XIII, Canon II, launches a terrible anathema in these words — if anyone says the substance of bread and wine remains with Christ’s Body and Blood, and denies that marvelous conversion of the whole substance of bread into the Body and of wine into the Blood (species alone remaining), which the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation, let him be anathema (pag. m. 130).
Stop before the proof that true divine Fundamentals make the limits — from Ephesians 4 (authoritative and ratiocinative).

source_text: Eadem verò Fundamentalia vera divinaque, Consociationis Ecclesiasticae limites conficere, probatur, tàm Autoritative, quam Ratiocinative.
english: That the same true, divine Fundamentals set the limits of church Consociation is proved two ways — by authority and by reason.

source_text: Autoritative ex Cap. 4. ad Ephes., rei probandae Loco quasi Communi reputando, totum insuper Fundamentum tàm Theoreticum à v. 1. ad 17. quàm Practicum à v. 17. ad fin. Cap. complexo, quando Apostolus v. 3. jubet servare unitatem Spiritûs in vinculo pacis, & unum Corpus Spiritumque, unum Corpus Spirituale constitui affirmat, ubi unus est Dominus, una fides, unum Baptisma, unus Deus & Pater omnium, qui est super omnes & per omnes & in omnibus v. 4. 5. 6.;
english: By authority: take Ephesians 4 as a standing commonplace for the point — covering the whole foundation, theoretical (vv. 1–17) and practical (v. 17 to the chapter’s end).

There the Apostle bids us keep the Spirit’s unity in the bond of peace (v. 3), and affirms one body and one Spirit — one spiritual body — where there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, above all, through all, and in all (vv. 4–6).

source_text: licèt deinceps & quod reliquum est, unicuique gratia data, etiam diversi gradûs, sit, secundum mensuram doni Christi v. 7. & alii constituti sint Apostoli, alii Prophetae v. 11. idque ad οἰκοδομὴν τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ad aedificationem Corporis Christi v. 12.
english: Yet afterward, and for what remains, grace is given to each — even in different measures — according to Christ’s gift (v. 7).
Some are set as apostles, others as prophets (v. 11), and that for the building up of Christ’s body (v. 12).

source_text: quò καταντήσωμεν οἱ πάντες εἰς τὴν ἑνότητα τῆς πίστεως καὶ ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ ὑιοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον, donec perveniamus omnes ad unam fidem [puta in omnibus & singulis] & in perfectum virum evadamus v. 13. non dimovendum vel circumagitandum omni ventô Doctrinae v. 14. intereà ἀληθεύοντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ in Charitate Veritati studentes v. 15.
english: The aim is that we all arrive at the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a full-grown man (v. 13) — not tossed by every wind of teaching (v. 14) —
meanwhile speaking truth in love, studying truth in charity (v. 15).

source_text: Ratiocinative: Quia in Fundamentalibus eoque necessariis praecipuisque Christianae Religionis dogmatibus unanimes, licèt in aliis minus fundamentalibus minusque necessariis dissentientes, ad majorem intereà perfectamque Unitatem contendentes, in Charitate, unum idemque Spirituale Corpus magis sunt, quàm non sunt; vel (quod eodem recurrit) unius ejusdemque Ecclesiae Christianae Consociatione continentur magis, quàm non continentur: Quandoquidem à potiori fit denominatio.
english: By reason: those agreed on the fundamental — and so necessary and chief — dogmas of the Christian religion, though they still differ on lesser points, yet press on toward fuller unity in charity.
They are more one spiritual body than not.
Or, what comes to the same, they are more held in the Consociation of one Christian church than they are shut out of it — for we name a thing from its greater part.

source_text: Sicuti verò hominibus accensentur & societate humana eâdem contineri putantur, qui corpore & animâ rationali praediti sunt, licèt quandoque & animae rationalis vis virtusque exigua perquam, & Corporis membra nonnulla multum deformata inveniantur; ita ejusdem Consociationis Ecclesiasticae participes aestimandi, qui Ecclesiae Christianae essentialia, tàm Theoretica, quam Practica servant, licèt cum erroribus pariter atque peccatis Christianam Religionem haud evertentibus, etiam benè multis, colluctentur.
english: Just as people with a body and a rational soul still count as human and as members of one society — even when the soul’s force is weak and some bodily members are badly misshapen —
so those who keep the church’s essentials, theoretical and practical, should be counted sharers in the same church Consociation,
even while they wrestle with many errors and sins that do not overturn the Christian religion.
Stop before §. IV (consensus and Consociation judged from the same fundamental principle).
